info.name: PROG2002 A2 - Charity Events API
info.description:
REST API for the charity events website.

Built for PROG2002 Web Development II, Assessment 2 (read-only) and extended for
Assessment 3 (the write endpoints, registrations and the admin view).

Data source : MySQL 8.4, database charityevents_db
Base URL    : http://localhost:3000/api
Offline     : with DATA_SOURCE=local the API mirrors the same seed data in memory

The A2 folders read the API. The A3 folder writes to it and is chained with
collection variables, so it has to run after them. Inside it:

  Events                       creates the event and saves newEventId, updates
                               it, reads it back, and shows the 400 and the 404
  Registrations                registers against it (saving registrationId),
                               proves the duplicate email is refused with a 409,
                               reads and edits the registration, proves the event
                               cannot be deleted while the registration exists
                               (409), deletes the registration, then deletes the
                               event with the 204 that the 409 was standing in
                               the way of
  Validation of the ticket     creates a small event to show that a registration
  allocation                   cannot exceed what is left of a tier, and removes
                               it again
  Admin view                   the same events seen regardless of status

Within a folder the requests run in the order shown, and across folders Postman
runs a folder's own requests after its sub-folders - which is why the requests
that depend on a registration live in the folder that creates it, even though the
delete being refused is a statement about /events. The whole collection can be run
top to bottom with the Collection Runner, and it leaves the database as it found
it.

Folder "Validation and error handling" keeps the A2 failures. The A3 failures sit
beside the resource they are about - the 400s and the 404 in "Events", the
duplicate-registration and blocked-delete 409s in "Registrations" - because each
one is a statement about that resource.

Suggested demo order for the video:
  1. Health check
  2. Home page listing (upcoming events)
  3. Search with all three criteria at once
  4. The deliberately invalid date range, to show the 400 response
  5. The suspended event, to show that it is hidden (404)
  6. Create an event, then register for it (201 and 201)
  7. The blocked delete (409), then delete the registration and the event (204)

Create an event, register an attendee for it, prove the delete is refused while that registration exists, then delete the registration and the event. Every id is passed along in a collection variable, so the folder can be run from top to bottom and leaves the database as it found it.

item.name: Events
item.description: The full C.R.U.D. cycle on /api/events: create, update, read the stored row back, and delete. The requests that are expected to fail are here too - the 400 for a missing field, the 400 for an empty update body, the 404 for an unknown id and the 409 for the blocked delete - because each one is a statement about this resource. The requests run in order and pass newEventId along in a collection variable.

item.name: POST /events  (create, and save the id)
item.description: Creates the event the rest of this folder works on and stores the new id in the collection variable newEventId, so every later request addresses the event this run created rather than a seeded one. The pre-request script settles one run id that the event name and the attendee email are both built from, which is what keeps the collection re-runnable: the name is always new and the email never collides with the unique key on (event_id, attendee_email).

item.name: Registrations
item.description: Registrations, the A3 resource that makes the delete rule worth demonstrating. A registration only exists inside an event, so it is created by posting to the event's sub-collection and addressed by its own URL afterwards. The folder registers against the event created in the sibling folder "Events", reads the registration back, edits it, and deletes it - which is what unblocks the event so that the last request of the collection can delete it with a 204.

item.name: DELETE /events/{{newEventId}}  (204, the event that was created)

The request before it - also in the folder "Registrations" - removed the registration, so the same URL that answered 409 while the registration existed answers 204 now, and the run leaves the database as it found it. item.name: Admin view
item.description: The admin view. These endpoints exist because the admin site has to see events the public site must never show, and it needs the dropdown lists for its forms. The list reads vw_all_events rather than vw_public_events, so a suspended event is included rather than hidden - which is the difference shown in one response here.

The keyword filter is set to "suspended" so the result is exactly the row the public API answers 404 for - the clearest way to show the difference between the two views in a single response.

item.name: Validation of the ticket allocation
item.description: One rule, on its own: a registration may not ask for more tickets than the chosen tier has left. It needs an event whose tier is genuinely nearly full, so it creates its own small event (capacity 1) rather than borrowing the main one, proves the 400, and deletes the event again. The folder runs after "Registrations" so that the amounts it reports are not confused with the registrations made there.

item.name: POST /events  (a small event for the allocation check)
item.description: Sets up the event the next request needs: one tier with a single place, so asking for more than one ticket must be refused. It is deliberately kept out of the main create request so that the event the rest of the collection works on stays the realistic one from the documentation, and it is deleted again at the end of this folder.

item.name: POST /events/{{allocationEventId}}/registrations  (more than remain)  -> 400
item.description: EXPECTED TO FAIL with 400. The tier has one place and the request asks for the largest quantity a single registration may contain, so the API counts what is left and refuses. error.details carries the remaining number and the tier name as extra keys beside field and message, which is what lets the form say "choose 1 or fewer" rather than merely "invalid" - and it is the same error.details shape the form already handles for a plain field failure.
